title: Exercises
subtitle: 44 hands-on exercises built for this exact lab, plus a bonus set on reading raw logs and cross-referencing real detections.

intro.text: These aren't generic "try Wazuh" tutorials — every one of them targets a real capability, a real rule ID, or a real bug documented elsewhere on this site. Half are defensive (read a dashboard, investigate an alert), half are offensive (run a real attack from Kali against your own lab and confirm detection).

intro.title: The golden rule, no exceptions
intro.text: Every exercise here targets only your own machines, on your own authorized network. Never a third party. Never a public IP that isn't yours. For brute-force exercises, always use a disposable test account with a handful of manual attempts — never a real account, never an automated wordlist against anything that matters.

toolSetup.title: One-time tool setup (on the Kali box)
toolSetup.code:
sudo apt update

# CrackMapExec / NetExec
sudo apt install -y netexec

# Impacket (Kerberoasting, psexec, etc.)
sudo apt install -y impacket-scripts

# Atomic Red Team needs PowerShell on Linux
sudo apt install -y powershell
pwsh -Command "Install-Module -Name powershell-yaml -Force -Scope CurrentUser"
pwsh -Command "IEX (IWR 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redcanaryco/invoke-atomicredteam/master/install-atomicredteam.ps1' -UseBasicParsing); Install-AtomicRedTeam -getAtomics"

# BloodHound needs its own infrastructure — see exercise A-8

items.title: Find the most recent alert from victim-linux
items.text: In Discover or Threat Hunting, find the most recent alert from the victim-linux agent, whatever the rule. Identify rule.id, rule.level, and summarize what rule.description says happened, in one sentence.

items.title: Count critical alerts in the media_isolation group
items.text: How many alerts with rule.level >= 12 and rule.groups:"media_isolation" exist in the last 30 days? Report the real number, plus the oldest and newest timestamps.

items.title: Which Suricata sensor talks the most?
items.text: Open the network-security dashboard and check the network-alerts-by-sensor panel. Which of the 8 sensors generated the most alerts in the last 30 days? Is that expected, given each machine's usage pattern?

items.title: Nmap scan against victim-linux
items.text: From kali-vm, run nmap -Pn against victim-linux's real IP. Confirm on the network-security dashboard whether the scan appeared, and on which sensor. If it didn't appear anywhere, explain why using the SPAN/loopback lessons from the Wazuh page.

items.title: Simulate a detectable SSH scan
items.text: Generate traffic that triggers the ET SCAN Potential SSH Scan OUTBOUND signature — several quick connection attempts to port 22. Find the alert in Discover and report data.src_ip, data.dest_ip, and rule.firedtimes.

items.title: The same event, seen by two sensors
items.text: Generate traffic between two machines that both run Suricata. Find the two documents generated for the same network event — one from each sensor — and explain why there are two records instead of one, using agent.name and data.flow_id.

items.title: The mystery IP
items.text: In the network-top-source-ips panel, identify an IP that doesn't correspond to any of the 8 known agents. What is it likely to be? Confirm using data.alert.signature.

items.title: Trigger a simulated ransomware detection
items.text: On victim-linux, create 3–5 test files in /srv/media/ingest, then rename all of them to end in .locked. Confirm rule 100200 fired at level 12.

items.title: Confirm isolation, failover, and forensic report
items.text: After exercise 8, confirm all three legs of the automated response: the isolation trigger in active-responses.log, the failover being logged, and a forensic report existing — with a matching incident_id across all three.

items.title: Restore and confirm reversibility
items.text: Revert the exercise-8 test files to their original state and confirm syscheck no longer reports a discrepancy. In one sentence, explain why testing reversibility matters for every simulation on this page.

items.title: Failed SSH login, three times
items.text: Using a disposable test account, attempt SSH login with the wrong password three times. Find the three corresponding alerts and check whether rule.level increased from the first to the third attempt.

items.title: Unusual sudo command and MITRE mapping
items.text: Run a command like sudo -u otheruser whoami on a Linux machine. Find the alert (rule 5407) and confirm rule.mitre.id shows T1548.003. Explain what this technique means, in one sentence.

items.title: Create an AD user and see if Wazuh noticed
items.text: On win-server-vm, create a new AD user via ADUC or New-ADUser. Look for a corresponding event (typically Event ID 4720). If nothing is found, that's still a valid result — investigate why AD auditing isn't enabled.

items.title: Domain logon with the wrong password
items.text: Using one of the existing domain test users, attempt a logon with the wrong password. Look for a failed-logon event (Event ID 4625) from win-server-vm and report whether it appeared.

items.title: Unusual PowerShell command on win10-vm
items.text: Run an encoded PowerShell command (powershell -enc <base64>). Find the event and identify which field shows the command was Base64-obfuscated.

items.title: Triage a CVE from scratch, the right way
items.text: Pick a Critical/High CVE not yet documented in the CVE Management page. Follow the full flow: read the description, check the vendor tracker, assess whether the component is actually used, decide fix/mitigate/accept, and document it.

items.title: Hunt a false positive from an outdated-version report
items.text: Check whether any listed kernel CVE points to a version different from what uname -r actually shows running — an orphaned kernel, exactly like the CVE-2026-31536 case. If found, restart the agent and confirm resync.

items.title: Build a new dashboard from scratch
items.text: Pick a focus area without its own dashboard yet — win-server-vm/AD, or PAM/sudo authentication across all machines. Build at least 3 visualizations (a Metric, a Line or Table, a Pie) and a named dashboard.

items.title: Configure a real Alerting monitor
items.text: Create a monitor checking every 5 minutes for more than 3 non-noise network alerts. Configure a level-2 trigger and wire it to a Notifications channel. Re-run exercise 5 and confirm the monitor fires.

items.title: Generate a PDF report of the network dashboard
items.text: Generate a PDF report of the network-security dashboard covering the last 7 days. Confirm the PDF matches what's on screen.

items.title: Reconstruct the timeline of a real incident
items.text: Pick a real network event already generated in this lab. Reconstruct the full timeline: origin machine, which sensors saw it, in what order, and elapsed time between the first and last document.

items.title: Investigate the tuning-rule leak
items.text: Rule 100101 is documented as not catching 100% of the noisy signature it targets. Investigate local_rules.xml, understand the exact condition, and propose a fix that closes the gap.

items.title: Host discovery across the whole subnet
items.text: Confirm an ICMP/ARP traffic spike from kali-vm across all sensors simultaneously — the signature of a full sweep vs. a single-target scan.

items.title: Full TCP port scan (all 65535 ports)
items.text: Compare to the standard ~1000-port scan already done — this takes much longer and should generate a larger alert volume. Report how long it took.

items.title: Service version and OS detection
items.text: This scan sends malformed packets on purpose to fingerprint the OS. Check for a signature different from the generic scan alert.

items.title: Vulnerability scripting scan (NSE)
items.text: Nmap's most aggressive scan — actively tests known vulnerabilities. Confirm a visibly higher alert volume, and compare Nmap's own findings against Wazuh's Vulnerability Detection module — they're different data sources and don't always agree.

items.title: SSH brute-force with Hydra
items.text: Prep: create a disposable test account beforehand — never use a real one. Find the repeated, rapid-sequence PAM authentication_failed alerts — this pattern differentiates a human mistyping a password from automated tooling.

items.title: RDP brute-force against Windows
items.text: Look for repeated failed-logon events (Event ID 4625) on win10-vm, and confirm Suricata also captured the repeated RDP traffic pattern on port 3389.

items.title: Password spraying against Active Directory
items.text: Unlike brute-force, spraying tries one password against many accounts specifically to avoid lockouts. Check the domain's lockout policy first (net accounts /domain). Look for repeated 4625 events from the same source against different accounts — the pattern that distinguishes spraying from brute-force.

items.title: User and SMB share enumeration
items.text: Find the SMB traffic (port 445) in Suricata, and if AD auditing is enabled, look for corresponding object-access events.

items.title: Kerberoasting — extracting service tickets
items.text: Only works if a service account with a registered SPN exists — an empty result is a valid outcome. If a ticket returns, look for Event 4769 with a weak encryption type.

items.title: Lateral movement via SMB (psexec-style)
items.text: A real lateral-movement technique via a temporary remote service. Only ever use the test account. Look for service creation (Event ID 7045) right before the remote execution — the classic evidence a SOC analyst looks for.

items.title: Map attack paths with BloodHound
items.code:
sudo apt install -y bloodhound neo4j
sudo neo4j start
bloodhound-python -u test-user -p test-pass -d domain.local -ns 192.168.178.163 -c all
items.text: Recon/analysis, not exploitation. Explore the imported graph for any path from a regular user to Domain Admins. "No obvious path" is also a valuable, documentable result.

items.title: Auxiliary service-version scanner
items.code: msfconsole -q -x "use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_version; set RHOSTS 192.168.178.163; run; exit"
items.text: auxiliary/scanner/* modules are recon, not exploitation — the safe starting point before any real exploit. Confirm the traffic appeared in the target's Suricata.

items.title: Exploit a CVE you've already identified yourself
items.text: Search your own Vulnerability Detection findings for a documented CVE with a real Metasploit module (search cve:YEAR-NUMBER). Snapshot the VM first. If none found exploitable, that's the expected — and worth documenting — result in most cases.

items.title: certutil as a disguised downloader/decoder
items.code:
certutil -encode file.txt file.b64
certutil -decode file.b64 out.txt
items.text: Find Sysmon Event ID 1 showing certutil.exe with the -decode parameter — a real pattern attackers use since certutil is a legitimate, Microsoft-signed binary.

items.title: PowerShell download cradle
items.text: The classic "download cradle" — fetch and execute in memory without saving to disk. Find the Sysmon event and confirm the full command line is readable, not obfuscated.

items.title: Local account discovery via native commands
items.code:
net user
net localgroup administrators
whoami /priv
items.text: Each command looks harmless alone — but the sequence (list users, list admins, check own privileges) is a post-exploitation recon pattern. Explain why sequence matters more than any single command in real triage.

items.title: T1059.001 — Suspicious PowerShell execution
items.text: Confirm the resulting Sysmon event and that the MITRE technique field matches what the framework announced.

items.title: T1003 — Credential access simulation
items.text: Simulates the Mimikatz-style behavior pattern (LSASS process access) safely, without extracting real credentials. Verify a process-access event on lsass.exe.

items.title: T1547 — Persistence via startup registry key
items.code:
Invoke-AtomicTest T1547.001
# always clean up after confirming detection:
Invoke-AtomicTest T1547.001 -Cleanup
items.text: Find the registry-modification event on the Run/RunOnce key, then confirm -Cleanup actually removed the entry.

items.title: T1078 — Valid account use at an unusual time
items.text: No special tool needed: log into a test domain account outside business hours. Apply the same reasoning as the "endpoint disappears" and "3AM alert" training cases — unusual timing is an aggravating factor even with valid credentials.

items.title: Real encryption of test files
items.code:
tar -czf ~/backup-pre-test.tar.gz -C /srv/media/ingest .
for f in /srv/media/ingest/test-*.txt; do
  openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -in "$f" -out "$f.enc" -k "test-key"
  sudo rm "$f"
done
items.text: Unlike a simple rename, this actually renders the content unreadable — closer to real ransomware behavior. Confirm rule 100200 fires for both the delete and the new .enc file, and that Active Response isolates the node normally.

items.title: Shadow copy deletion (anti-recovery)
items.text: Snapshot the VM before running this — there is no undo. This is literally what real ransomware families run to prevent recovery. On its own, with no other context, this command should already be treated as a critical indicator. Does your environment have a specific rule for it? If not, that's a real gap to document.

sections.title: P. Reading Real Logs & Cross-Referencing Detections (bonus)
sections.intro: Beyond the 44 structured exercises above: the skill that actually separates a junior analyst from a senior one is reading raw data directly, without waiting for a dashboard to summarize it — and confirming that different tools looking at the same event actually agree.

items.title: Read a raw Suricata eve.json line, no dashboard
items.text: SSH into a machine running Suricata and tail -f /var/log/suricata/eve.json (or the platform-equivalent path) while generating traffic from another machine. Identify the alert.signature, src_ip, dest_ip and flow_id fields directly in the raw JSON, before it ever reaches Wazuh's index.

items.title: Correlate a real external scan against your public IP
items.text: This lab had a genuine (not simulated) ET SCAN Potential SSH Scan OUTBOUND alert fire from kali-vm during testing, with firedtimes climbing past 180 in a few minutes and zero response from the destination. Reproduce a similar investigation: find a real outbound scan alert in your own environment, and determine from bytes_toclient (or its absence) whether the target actually responded — a genuine security-posture signal, not just a scan record.

items.title: Reconstruct an event from full_log alone
items.text: Pick any alert and ignore every structured field except full_log. Reconstruct, in plain English, exactly what happened using only the raw log line — the skill needed for the (common, real) case where a log format has no dedicated decoder yet.

items.title: Build a 24-hour "quiet baseline"
items.text: Pick one agent and record, hour by hour, what a completely normal day of alerts looks like: volume, top signatures, typical rule levels. This baseline is what makes an actual anomaly recognizable later — without it, every alert looks equally suspicious.

items.title: Compare a scanning tool's own output against what got detected
items.text: Run any scan from this page with verbose/output-file options (e.g. nmap -oA), then compare the tool's own report of what it did against what Wazuh/Suricata actually logged. Are they identical? If Wazuh saw fewer events than the tool actually sent, that's a real detection-coverage gap worth understanding, not just a mismatch to ignore.

items.title: Read auditd logs directly with ausearch
items.text: On a Linux endpoint, trigger an auditd rule (e.g. edit /etc/passwd, or attempt a privileged command) and read the result with ausearch -k <key> directly on the host, before it's parsed by Wazuh's decoder. Compare the raw audit fields to what ends up in the Wazuh alert — what gets kept, and what gets dropped?

items.title: Trace one incident across three tools
items.text: Pick a level 7+ alert. Find it in three places: the raw Wazuh alert (Discover), the TheHive alert it generated automatically, and — if you promote it — the resulting case. Confirm the incident tells the exact same story in all three, and note anything that got lost or changed in translation between them.
